# 153 — ONLYOFFICE capability parity, derived

**Status:** live. Every table below is GENERATED by `tools/opendoc-parity` from two
inventories and a human map, and `cargo test -p opendoc-parity` fails when the
committed document is not what a fresh run produces. Edit the map, re-run
`cargo run -p opendoc-parity -- write`, commit both.

## Why this document exists

Parity with ONLYOFFICE Docs has reached this project as scattered one-off
observations — a control missing here, a dialog behaving differently there.
`docs/130` is the only systematic comparison there has been, and it says so
itself: an analysis, stamped with the commit it was measured at, hand-written and
therefore already ageing on the day it landed. `docs/149` is the exception that
proves the point — it is generated, and it covers ONE axis, the host's
configuration surface.

The missing thing is a **capability** matrix that is derived rather than
hand-kept. `SKILL` §8 says counts in documents here must be derived, because
hand-maintained ones have drifted into false public claims twice; §9 rule 1 says
a published number is generated from a committed artifact or it is not published.
This document is that matrix, under those rules.

## How it is derived

Three inputs, two of them mechanical.

| Side | Where it comes from | Read when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **OpenDoc** | `webapp/src/host_contract.mjs` — `COMMAND_CONTRACT` and `COMMAND_FAMILIES` — plus grep anchors into named files for capabilities that are not host commands | live, on every run |
| **ONLYOFFICE** | `tools/opendoc-parity/data/onlyoffice-surface.json`, extracted from their checkout | at extraction; re-verified by `extract --check` |
| **The map** | `tools/opendoc-parity/data/capabilities.json` — the human reading | hand-authored |

**Our side is never snapshotted.** It is read from the module that implements it,
every time the matrix is generated or checked, because a snapshot of our own
surface would be exactly the second hand-kept table that drifts. The parse is
strict: an unrecognised declaration inside `COMMAND_CONTRACT` is an error rather
than a skip, since a lenient parse would under-report us.

`COMMAND_CONTRACT` can carry that weight because it is not a documentation table.
`webapp/tests/e2e/host-contract.spec.mjs` drives the editor through five states
and asserts **both** directions — every command the editor offers resolves in the
contract, and every contract row is offered by the editor. So an id in the
contract is a capability a user can reach, and a capability we ship is an id in
the contract.

**Their side is identifiers only.** Their code is AGPL-3.0 and their checkouts
live outside this repository; nothing of theirs is vendored here. The snapshot
holds control names, locale KEY names, engine API method names and boot-flag
names, each with the file and line it was read from. No English label, no source
line and no translated string is copied.

**The verdict is never written down.** Each row states what evidence to look for
on each side; the verdict falls out of whether that evidence resolves. A row that
says *we do not have this* is expressed as an assertion — it names the command
ids that must NOT be in the contract — so the day somebody ships one, the guard
fails and the document cannot go on understating us. That direction matters as
much as the other: `docs/105` CQ-005 still reads "no i18n seam at all" while
nineteen locales ship, and CQ-010 reads "no embed surface" while
`packages/opendoc-embed` exists.

## What this method cannot establish

Stated plainly, because understating a method's limits is the same defect as
overstating its results.

* **Semantic equivalence is a human reading.** That their `btnDropCap` and our
  `insert.dropCap` are the same capability is a judgement. The tool checks both
  anchors still exist; it cannot check they mean the same thing. Every row in the
  map is therefore a claim somebody made and somebody else can dispute.
* **Depth is not graded by presence.** Two products can both have a drop-cap
  dialog and offer different fields in it. `Parity` is about the capability, not
  about every option inside it; where the depth differs the row is `Partial` and
  the note says what is missing.
* **Our family members are not enumerable statically.** `COMMAND_FAMILIES`
  prefixes such as `table.`, `style.` and `format.family.` are populated at run
  time from the document and the font inventory, so a row resting on one of them
  cites the family and names the member in its note.
* **Their absence cannot be cited to a line.** A row claiming they lack something
  records the search that establishes it, so a reader with their tree can re-run
  it.
* **Their half is not CI-gated, and this document does not pretend otherwise.**
  CI has no ONLYOFFICE checkout, so `cargo test` verifies our side live and their
  side against the committed snapshot. Re-verifying the snapshot against their
  tree is `cargo run -p opendoc-parity -- extract --reference <dir> --check`, and
  it runs on a machine that has their source.

## What their boot controller decides, derived

Not hand-typed. The extractor records every `appOptions` flag in
`apps/documenteditor/main/app/controller/Main.js` together with the gates its
expression mentions, so the fair-comparison exclusions `docs/130` had to write out
by hand now fall out of the extraction.

Fourteen flags are gated on `canLicense` — a licence result the **document server**
issues during the handshake — and `isEdit` is one of them:

```js
this.appOptions.isEdit = this.appOptions.canLicense && this.appOptions.canEdit
                         && this.editorConfig.mode !== 'view';
```

So their web client does not decide for itself that it may edit; a server tells
it. `canComments`, `canReview`, `canEditStyles`, `canUseHistory`, `canUseMailMerge`
and the three permission-group flags carry the same condition. Three more flags —
`canPreviewPrint`, `canQuickPrint`, `isSignatureSupport` — are true only inside
their desktop shell, so they are not web-parity gaps at all.

This is the third structural advantage in `SKILL` §1 stated as a measurement
rather than as a slogan: a capability we ship with no server in the loop against
one of theirs that a server has to authorise is graded **Ours, ungated**, not
`Parity`.

## The tally

<!-- @generated parity-tally -->
| Verdict | Rows | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parity | 1 | both products ship it, and both anchors resolve |
| Ours, ungated | 1 | we ship it with no server in the loop; theirs is behind `canLicense` (a licence result the document server issues) or the desktop shell |
| Ours only | 0 | we ship it and their tree has no such surface |
| Partial | 0 | we ship part of it; the row says what is missing |
| Gap | 0 | their standalone browser session ships it and we do not |
| Theirs, server-gated | 0 | their side needs a server or the desktop shell, and we lack it too |
| **Total graded** | **2** | every row below |
<!-- @end parity-tally -->

## Open gaps, ranked by what a document user hits

Rank 1 is a capability a person reaches for constantly; rank 5 is specialist.
Ranked by use, not by how easy the work is. Each row is a normal change with its
own guard and mutation proof, and every capability must be reachable from at
least two surfaces (`SKILL` §10).

<!-- @generated parity-gaps -->
_No open gaps._
<!-- @end parity-gaps -->

## The matrix

`Ours` and `Theirs` cite the evidence the verdict was computed from. A citation
that stops resolving fails the build rather than quietly downgrading a row.

| Capability | Verdict | Ours | Theirs | Note |

| Bold | Parity | `format.bold` | `btnBold` | — |

### Review, proofing and collaboration (1 rows)

| Capability | Verdict | Ours | Theirs | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Related

* `docs/130` — the hand-written toolbar gap analysis this generalises and
  supersedes for capability questions. Its control COUNTS remain the better
  source for "how many controls are on which tab".
* `docs/149` — the host CONFIGURATION surface, option by option, also generated.
  The two do not overlap: 149 grades what a host may configure, 153 grades what a
  person may do.
* `docs/12` — the competitive analysis.
* `docs/105`, `docs/106`, `docs/104` — the audit rows, the roadmap and the defect
  queue. A gap here becomes a row there when it is picked up, not before.
